Global asym bound notes
=======================

The biggest problem is probably that Asym(G₀) is not numerically PSD (smallest
eigval, from Sean's tests (TODO: retest this ourselves in the full space) is
roughly -1e-6, or -1e-7.

LHS and RHS for global asym multiplier bounds 
---------------------------------------------

**The following is with χ = 11.098 + 0.005i ⇒  ζ = 2463.36208.**

When I use random vectors for the (L, R) formulation, I need a regularization of
1e-10 or 1e-9 and get α > -0.0008. With the RSVD seed, I only need 1e-14
regularization and get the same bound (I sometimes can get away with 0). I
cannot get it to converge for the (L, -R) formulation with random vectors. For
the RSVD seed with the (L, -R) formulation, the Krylov method stagnates (note:
does not *not* converge, just takes infinite time) for all regularizations. The
same is true of the random vector seeds. *NOTE:* The reason to try random
vectors vs RSVD seed is to check to see if the RSVD basis might be missing some
directions where one of the matrices is indefinite and the Krylov method might
not be able to find it (this is not observed for the (L, R) formulation though;
to be confirmed for the (R, -L) formulation).

Sweeping α and looking at λₘᵢₙ(α lhs - (α²/(ζ*(ζ - α))) rhs) in the full space
------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Sweeping over α from -1e-2 to -1e-7 in the full space, the zero crossing of the
global asym S operator (using `eigsolve`'s `:SR` with `tol=1e-10`) is between
-1e-3 and -6.8e-4, which is consistent with the bounds from the generalized
eigenvalue problem.

Full space generalized eigenvalue problem
-----------------------------------------

Plugging in α = -0.0008441507302211897 into (Ω, S(α)) gives us a maximum
generalized eigenvalue of 3.634359611614412e8, which gives us 29507.3 in power
units. Note that the smallest eigenvalue of S for that multiplier is
1.102099725965505e-14.

Ideas
-----

- Maybe we should augment the basis at every iteration in the full space
optimizer with the converged maximum geneigvectors and the minimum eigevectors
of S?

Old Stuff
=========

Notes
-----
I've noticed that, for a given k, if I warm start the multipliers for NLopt with
the multipliers from k-1, the optimization is much better, but the resulting
multipliers look weirder (I think this is finding a subspace optimal solution
that does not generalize well). When I don't warm start them (I only seed them
with the multiplier from global asym and set the others to 0), I don't get
monotonically decaying bounds, but the global asym multiplier does not change
that much. When I warm start them, the global asym multiplier changes a lot (a
factor of 100). The warm stared bounds are (more) monotonically decaying though.
I don't know what to make of this.

FULL SPACE OPTIMIZATION
-----------------------

For global asym, I ran a full space optimization routine (on k=1) using the
generalized eigenvalue problem formulation and got these results:

μ₀ = 4.5500793766998553e8 (36942.026619975055 in power units)
diagonal constraint = -1.0000002682137688 (< 0 means feasible)
Schur complement constraint = -5.852144607276109e-8 (< 0 means feasible)
α₁ = -0.0006607076270081298 (global asym multiplier)

Plugging α₁ into the reduced basis, we get:
μ₀ = 5854.451248984944 (0.4753220240351304 in power units)
diagonal constraint = -1.0000002682137688 (< 0 means feasible)
Schur complement constraint = -1.89581030943892e-7 (< 0 means feasible)
Note that this is only 1.5 times as large as the optimized result in the reduced
basis.

In the full space, the vector associated with the optimized solution is the
generalized eigenvector of the pencil (Ω, S). Let v be this vector. Here is what
I have found about this solution:
‖Ωv‖ = 150.1083423851104 
‖Sv‖ = 3.299027076936963e-7
Note that ‖Ωv‖ / ‖Sv‖ = 4.55e8, so it looks like
the solution is dominated by the nullspace of S.

In the reduced basis, the vector associated with its own optimized result is way
less dominated by the nullspace of S:
‖Ωv‖ = 34.449745329084955
‖Sv‖ = 0.008810699561525713

TODO: We can try and use the inferred μ₁ = -3.868080592151624 in another formulation

I took \alpha_1^U and evaluated it in the full space and got a massive value of
1.8e8. Note that the solution was technically infeasible (minimum eigenvector of S
was -1e-7, so I added 1e-7*I to S to get this value). The norm of Sv for this
multiplier was on the order 1e-6 and the norm of \Omega v was on the order of
152.

When I look at the spectrum of S at their optimal values, I see that there are
many singular values near 1e-7 (note that these computations are done with
Float64). In the reduced basis, the smallest eigenvalue is 2e-7. There is a
sharp drop at some point in the spectrum to this 2e-7 (the top eigenvalue is on
the order of 3.9e-3). In the full space, at its own optimum, the smallest
eigenvalue is 1e-24, but there is a sharp drop off from 1e-7 to 1e-24, so I
would say the smallest eigenvalue is 1.3e-7. The top eigenvalue is on the order
of 1.7e-3, and there is also a sharp drop off to 1e-7 in the top part of the
spectrum there.

I don't really want to try and look at the original SDP because the way I have
things coded up right now it would be complicated to evaluate the constraint of
the SDP.

WHAT I AM TRYING
----------------

I am running the full space optimization with region constraints:
- global sym/asym
- source sym/asym
- receiver sym/asym
If these bounds looks closer to the RSVD bounds, then maybe the RSVD bounds are
capturing something about region constraints.

I will also try and vary the size of the basis

## Region constraint results

### Subspace results

subspace_constraint_bounds = [3.2412706051793663]
subspace_constraint_multipliers = [-0.001956635030868307 0.0006600622088254374 -0.00023046374132124233 0.0002764628874280328 -0.00024349634778134363 0.000297635970690017]

### Full space results

Couldn't find a feasible point. Sean suggested adding the eigenvector of the
smallest eigenvalue of S to the basis. This should help the optimizer find the
feasible region. The idea is to solve in the basis, check the solution in the
fullspace and add the eigenvector of the smallest eigenvalue of S if the point
is infeasible. Repeat this until a feasible point is found. Then maybe we can do
some fullspace optimization if we want.

It might be interesting to also add some of the top eigenvectors of \Omega to
the basis as well. We can try this when we have `extend!` working.
